overview: Bunge Global SA is a 200+ year old premier agribusiness solutions company that connects farmers to consumers by purchasing, storing, transporting, processing, and distributing agricultural commodities and related products for the food, feed, and fuel industries. It operates through four reportable segments -- Soybean Processing and Refining, Softseed Processing and Refining, Tropical Oils and Specialty Ingredients (renamed from Other Oilseeds Processing and Refining in Q1 2026), and Grain Merchandising and Milling -- with facilities in more than 50 countries. Following its $18 billion combination with Viterra Limited, completed July 2, 2025, Bunge significantly expanded its global grain origination, storage, and logistics footprint, particularly in Canada, Australia, South America, and the Black Sea region; the company is domiciled in Geneva, Switzerland (redomesticated from Bermuda in November 2023) with corporate headquarters in Chesterfield, Missouri.

business_model.summary: Bunge earns margin on the purchase, storage, transportation, processing (crushing), refining, and merchandising of agricultural commodities -- primarily soybeans, canola/rapeseed, sunflower seed, corn, wheat, and other oilseeds -- converting them into protein meal, vegetable oils, biodiesel/renewable diesel feedstocks, and milled products (flour, bakery mixes). Profitability is driven by processing margins (the spread between commodity input costs and meal/oil output prices, i.e., the 'crush margin'), merchandising/trading margins on grain flows, volumes processed and sold, capacity utilization, and ancillary trade structured finance and risk management services. Revenue is largely transactional/commodity-pass-through (very high revenue with thin margins) rather than recurring, though scale, asset utilization, and farmer relationships provide some stability. Customers are overwhelmingly B2B: animal feed manufacturers, livestock/poultry producers, biofuel companies, other oilseed processors, food manufacturers, bakery/food-service companies, and grocery/retail channels (B2C only for a modest packaged/branded oils business).

revenue_streams.name: Tropical Oils and Specialty Ingredients (fka Other Oilseeds)

business_model.customer_type: B2B (animal feed manufacturers, livestock/poultry producers, biofuel companies, other processors, food manufacturers, bakers) with a small B2C packaged/specialty oils tail
business_model.geographic_mix: Soybean processing capacity: 47% South America, 25% North America, 15% Asia-Pacific, 13% Europe. Softseed processing capacity: 53% Europe, 30% North America, 13% South America, 4% Asia-Pacific. Post-Viterra, employee base is 43% South America, 24% EMEA, 20% North America, 13% Asia-Pacific; operations span 50+ countries with major exposure to Brazil, Argentina, the US, Canada, and Ukraine.

competitive_position.market_position: One of the 'ABCD' oligopoly of global grain/oilseed traders (ADM, Bunge, Cargill, LDC/Dreyfus) plus COFCO and Wilmar as expanded competitors; Bunge describes itself as a leading global oilseed processor/producer of vegetable oils and protein meal (by capacity and volume), a leading global grain merchandiser (by volume), a leading seller of packaged plant-based oils worldwide (by sales), and a leading producer/seller of wheat flours and bakery mixes in South America (by volume). The Viterra acquisition materially increased scale in origination, storage, and logistics, especially in Canada, Australia, and the Black Sea/South America corridors.

moat_factors.description: 35 soybean processing plants, 29 softseed plants, and large refining/packaging networks across North/South America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific give cost and logistics advantages that are difficult for smaller players to replicate.

298 commodity storage facilities, 29 export port terminals, and extensive rail/barge/ocean freight infrastructure (expanded materially by Viterra's Canadian, Australian, and Black Sea assets) create a hard-to-replicate physical network and origination advantage.

A small number of global trading houses (ADM, Bunge, Cargill, LDC) dominate global grain/oilseed flows, providing some pricing discipline and barriers to new entrants, though the business remains intensely price-competitive on commodity products.

Bunge provides prepaid commodity purchase financing to farmers (particularly in Brazil, ~$835 million outstanding at YE2025) to secure raw material supply, deepening origination relationships but also creating counterparty credit risk.
Combination created a larger, more globally diversified platform across four segments and geographies, reducing single-region/single-crop concentration risk relative to pre-merger Bunge.

weaknesses: Commodity nature of products means intense price competition and limited pricing power; competition is based on price, location, and logistics rather than brand
Thin margins on a very large revenue base make earnings highly sensitive to crush-margin swings, weather, and trade policy
Heavy leverage following the debt-funded Viterra acquisition reduces financial flexibility relative to less-levered peers
Significant emerging-market and geopolitical exposure (Ukraine war, Brazil/Argentina currency and tax risk, China trade policy)
Integration risk and execution complexity from combining two large, geographically dispersed organizations

growth_drivers: Viterra integration delivering cost synergies -- raised from an original $250 million target to $350 million, with ~$190 million realized in 2026 (ahead of the original $175 million plan) -- plus longer-term commercial synergies from combined origination and logistics networks
Expanded global footprint in Canada, Australia, and the Black Sea/South America grain corridors from Viterra, diversifying origination and giving more flexibility to serve shifting global trade flows

Biofuel policy tailwinds: higher U.S. EPA Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO) blending mandates released in 2026 reduced policy uncertainty and supported crush margins; renewable diesel/biodiesel feedstock demand (including the Bunge Chevron Ag Renewables JV) continues to grow
Record/favorable soybean crush margins in 2026, aided by firmer vegetable oil prices and strong biofuel demand, which drove multiple upward revisions to full-year adjusted EPS guidance
Global protein demand growth (poultry, pork, livestock feed) supporting long-term grain and oilseed meal demand

New capacity additions, e.g., the new oilseed processing line at Destrehan, Louisiana starting production in Q4 2026, and the pending acquisition of lecithin/soy protein concentrate/crush assets from International Flavors & Fragrances (Solae), expected to close in 2026
Continued capital return program: $3.0 billion share repurchase authorization approved March 2026, and a raised quarterly dividend ($0.72/share, up 3% from $0.70)

business.description: Agricultural commodity prices are volatile and sensitive to weather, crop yields, farmer planting decisions, and global supply/demand; adverse weather (droughts, hurricanes, low river levels) can disrupt supply, transportation, and operating results.

Highly competitive, price-driven markets with product substitution risk; competitors have added crushing/refining capacity, and renewable diesel demand has drawn new entrants (traditional petroleum companies) into feedstock refining competition.

Bunge operates four oilseed crushing facilities, two export terminals, and numerous grain elevators in Ukraine (though <2% of consolidated total assets/liabilities); ongoing war creates risk of property damage, business disruption, and cyberattack.
Cyclical industry with periods of overcapacity investment followed by oversupply that compresses crush margins and processing economics.

financial.description: Total debt balance was $14.05 billion at YE2025 (up materially from pre-deal levels due to assumed Viterra debt and acquisition financing); short-seller commentary (e.g., Spruce Point) has flagged net debt/EBITDA estimated as high as ~5.7x on some methodologies, materially above historical norms, with higher net interest expense ($628 million in 2025 vs. $471 million in 2024) weighing on net income.

Primary exposures to the Brazilian real, Canadian dollar, euro, and Chinese yuan/renminbi affect translated revenue/expenses and farm economics; working capital and borrowing needs rise with commodity prices.
Bunge advances capital to Brazilian farmers (~$835 million outstanding at YE2025) secured by crops/land, exposing it to crop-failure and farmer-default risk.
Ongoing Brazilian indirect tax claims (ICMS ~$160 million, PIS/COFINS ~$598 million as of Q3 2026) and labor/civil claims represent contingent liabilities.

regulatory.description: Earnings are sensitive to U.S. EPA Renewable Volume Obligations and other biofuel blending mandates in Brazil, Argentina, the EU and elsewhere; policy delays or reversals create significant earnings uncertainty, as acknowledged by management ('policy decisions, including biofuels and trade, remain in flux').

US-China agricultural trade disputes and tariffs on soybeans and other commodities can disrupt trade flows and pricing; a late-2025 trade thaw (China resuming large-scale US soybean purchases) reduced near-term risk, but policy remains subject to reversal.

regulatory.risk: EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) and sustainability reporting
regulatory.description: EUDR enforcement (delayed to December 2026) will require proof that palm oil, soy, and derived products are deforestation-free; EU CSRD sustainability disclosure rules (delayed to FY2027 for Bunge) and California's Climate Accountability Package add compliance costs.
Periods of high food/fertilizer prices have historically increased antitrust and competition-law scrutiny of large agribusiness traders.

macro.description: Demand for agricultural commodities and food products is sensitive to global GDP growth, consumer spending, and a prolonged Chinese economic slowdown.

Operating costs (electricity, natural gas, coal, diesel) and biofuel product pricing are tied to petroleum prices; renewable diesel/biodiesel margins depend on the spread between feedstock costs and fuel prices.
A hypothetical 100 bps increase in reference rates (e.g., SOFR) would increase interest expense by approximately $148 million on variable-rate debt as of Q3 2026.

execution.description: Combining two large, geographically dispersed organizations carries risk of failing to realize anticipated cost/commercial synergies, higher-than-expected integration costs, key staff attrition, and a longer-than-expected integration timeline; management expects the integration to continue in phases over several years.

Former Viterra shareholders Glencore (~17%), CPP Investments (~14%), and BCI (~3%) hold board nomination rights and collectively ~34% of shares, giving them significant influence over corporate actions and potentially deterring alternative change-of-control transactions.
Recent executive changes include a new Chief Operating Officer (Julio Garros, December 2025) and realignment of sustainability/government affairs leadership following the Viterra close.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global agribusiness/oilseed processing demand is supported by long-term population growth, rising protein consumption (poultry/pork/livestock feed), and growing biofuel/renewable diesel feedstock demand, but near-term crush margins are highly sensitive to biofuel policy decisions (US EPA RVOs, Brazilian/Argentine biodiesel mandates) and global trade flows (US-China soybean trade).
macro_factors.cyclicality: High within a given year/season (seasonal harvest cycles, though geographically diversified between hemispheres) and moderately cyclical across years as crush margins swing with policy, weather, and supply/demand imbalances; management has flagged 'limited visibility' given macro and policy uncertainty.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate -- elevated post-Viterra debt load ($14.05 billion total debt at YE2025, ~$16.7-18.3 billion by Q3 2026 including new senior notes issuances) increases sensitivity to rate changes; a 100bps move affects variable-rate interest expense by ~$148 million.
key_input_costs: Energy (electricity, natural gas, coal, diesel, bunker fuel)

recent_developments.event: Completed the $18 billion combination with Viterra Limited (stock-and-cash deal; ~65.6 million Bunge shares worth ~$5.3 billion plus ~$1.9-2.0 billion cash), creating a substantially larger global agribusiness platform and assuming significant Viterra debt.
Cost synergy target raised from the original $250 million to $350 million; ~$190 million realized in 2026, ahead of the original $175 million plan for the year.

Full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance raised sharply from $7.50-$8.00 to $9.00-$9.50 following a strong Q1 beat, driven by favorable crush margins and reduced biofuel policy uncertainty after EPA released higher blending mandates.
Other Oilseeds Processing and Refining segment renamed Tropical Oils and Specialty Ingredients (no change to segment composition).
Board approved a new $3.0 billion share repurchase program with an indefinite term.
Shareholders approved a $2.88/share annual dividend (quarterly installments of $0.72), a 3% increase over the prior $2.80/$0.70 rate.
Entered an asset purchase agreement to acquire lecithin, soy protein concentrate, and crush assets from International Flavors & Fragrances (Solae); expected to close in 2026.
Entered an agreement (March 2025) to sell the European margarines and spreads business; completion expected in 2026, subject to regulatory approval.
Completed the sale of the North America corn milling business; also completed divestiture of 40% of Spanish subsidiary BISA to Repsol SA (March 2025, retaining a controlling interest).

Completed divestiture of Bunge's 50% interest in the BP Bunge Bioenergia joint venture (sugar and bioenergy), consistent with Bunge no longer presenting a separate Sugar & Bioenergy segment as of January 1, 2025.

Reported Q3 2026 results: adjusted EPS of $2.56 (vs. $2.27 prior year), adjusted segment EBIT of $997 million (vs. $924 million); raised/maintained full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $9.25-$9.75, narrowed effective tax rate guidance to 23-25%, and guided net interest expense to $640-$670 million; production began at the new Destrehan, Louisiana oilseed processing line after quarter-end.

US-China trade tensions eased in late 2025 with China resuming large-scale US soybean purchases (reported commitment of at least 25 million metric tons annually starting 2026) alongside mutual tariff reductions, easing a key overhang on US origination economics.

items.notes: Up from the prior $9.00-$9.50 range (itself raised sharply from an initial $7.50-$8.00 after a strong Q1 2026 beat), reflecting favorable soybean crush margins and reduced biofuel policy uncertainty following EPA's higher Renewable Volume Obligation mandates.
Narrowed range provided alongside Q3 2026 results.
Reflects higher post-Viterra debt levels including new senior notes issuances in March and August 2026.
~$190 million realized in 2026, ahead of the original $175 million plan for the year; management continues to pursue opportunities to accelerate the synergy timeline.
3% increase from the prior $0.70/share quarterly rate, approved by shareholders May 20, 2026.
Approved March 9, 2026, following completion of the prior buyback program; no shares were repurchased in Q3 2026 itself.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Gregory Heckman has emphasized that the Viterra integration is running ahead of plan on cost synergies and has strengthened Bunge's ability to serve increasingly complex global food, feed, and fuel markets, while cautioning that 'policy decisions, including biofuels and trade, remain in flux' and that 'visibility remains limited given ongoing macroeconomic conditions.' Management has pointed to strong Soybean and Softseed Processing and Refining segment performance, the new Destrehan, Louisiana crush facility, and narrowing uncertainty around U.S. biofuel blending mandates as key drivers of the raised 2026 outlook.

bull_case: Viterra combination creates a scaled, more diversified global agribusiness platform with an expanded origination and logistics network (Canada, Australia, Black Sea, South America) that is difficult for smaller competitors to replicate

Cost synergies are running ahead of plan ($190 million realized in 2026 vs. $175 million planned) with a raised $350 million target, providing a multi-year earnings tailwind independent of commodity cycles

2026 crush margins and biofuel policy clarity (higher EPA RVOs) have driven repeated upward revisions to adjusted EPS guidance (from $7.50-$8.00 to $9.25-$9.75), evidencing significant positive earnings momentum
Secular tailwinds from rising global protein demand and growing renewable diesel/biofuel feedstock demand support long-term volume growth across crush and merchandising businesses

Substantial capital return program ($3.0 billion buyback authorization plus a raised, 3%-higher dividend) signals management confidence and returns capital to shareholders even amid the large Viterra debt load
bear_case: Leverage taken on to fund the Viterra acquisition is elevated, with total debt near $14-18 billion and net debt/EBITDA estimated by some analysts (including short-seller Spruce Point) as high as ~5.7x, well above historical norms, raising interest expense and reducing financial flexibility

Earnings are a thin margin spread on a very large commodity revenue base, making them highly sensitive to reversible swings in crush margins, biofuel policy (EPA RVOs), and trade policy -- the recent EPS guidance upgrades could reverse quickly if crude oil prices fall or policy stalls

Viterra integration carries multi-year execution risk: realizing commercial synergies (versus the more easily quantified cost synergies) is described by management itself as difficult to quantify, and integration costs, systems consolidation, and cultural integration could take longer or cost more than planned

Significant geopolitical and trade-policy exposure, including ongoing Ukraine war risk to four crushing facilities and export terminals, and a US-China soybean trade relationship that, while currently thawed, has proven volatile and could deteriorate again

Large concentrated shareholders (Glencore ~17%, CPP Investments ~14%) with board nomination rights could create governance friction or limit strategic flexibility, while Swiss corporate law constraints add complexity to capital management and shareholder rights relative to US-domiciled peers
